attachments.title: Nootrobox Launches Its “Smart Drugs” Subscription Service
attachments.text:
Subscription-based &ldquo;box of the month&rdquo; services have been fairly hit-or-miss so far. While some&nbsp;like Birchbox are still going strong, elsewhere, smaller startups &ndash; and even experiments from the world&rsquo;s largest retailer, Walmart &ndash; have faded away. But a new company called Nootrobox is giving the subscription biz a shot anyway by targeting those interested in&nbsp;nutritional supplements &ndash; specifically brain nutrients and &ldquo;smart drugs&rdquo; also called nootropics.
Brain drugs that make you more productive? Sounds like something startup founders would be interested in. After all, it&rsquo;s like the nutritional complement to Soylent, the Metamucil-like beverage pitched as a more efficient replacement for food&nbsp;that&rsquo;s becoming&nbsp;known&nbsp;among the &ldquo;work hard/study hard&rdquo; crowd of engineers and college students.
The new startup&nbsp;is the latest from ex-Googler (now pro photographer and adjunct&nbsp;professor)&nbsp;Michael Brandt, and co-founder&nbsp;Geoffrey Woo, who previously launched Y Combinator-backed&nbsp;Glassmap, a location-based social app acquired by&nbsp;Groupon last year.
Woo, a Stanford grad, is currently an Entrepreneur-In-Residence (EIR) at Foundation Capital.

The two have developed&nbsp;a supplement they&rsquo;re calling RISE by collating materials and studies about ingredients used in other&nbsp;nootropics. Its stack is designed for &ldquo;memory, focus and energy,&rdquo; like a pill form of a cup of coffee, Woo explains. The company follows the FDA&rsquo;s current &ldquo;Good Manufacturing Practices&rdquo; guidelines and sources its ingredients stateside. Ingredient details, including the peer-reviewed studies, are here, but include bacopa monnieri, theanine, and caffeine. The pills are sold in packs starting at $9/month ranging up to $53/month.
The product alone is not really the draw of Nootrobox. Nutritional&nbsp;supplements are fairly common, and can be found at local health food stores, and other online and offline specialty shops. Nootrobox&rsquo;s selling point is that it&rsquo;s&nbsp;aiming to stack multiple compounds in one pill to help out those who are really into their supplements, and were previously&nbsp;making their own stacks using different buckets of powder.
&ldquo;Nootrobox offers &lsquo;stacks in a capsule&rsquo; so we make it super accessible and convenient,&rdquo; explains Woo.
But really, the startup is about getting these regular&nbsp;nutritional supplement consumers&nbsp;to buy their products differently &ndash; i.e., on subscription.
&ldquo;The space is very early so a lot of the market tendencies are being established by early players. &nbsp;E-commerce, anecdotally, is a popular channel because the demographics for online buyers, nootropics enthusiasts, and young professionals/students overlap broadly,&rdquo; Woo&nbsp;says.
The company&rsquo;s thesis is that the nootropics section of the overall nutritional supplements market will grown at an outsized pace within the larger trend. Nutritional supplements are expected to reach $60 billion by 2021, to give you an idea.

The startup&rsquo;s pitch of course fits well into this ongoing&nbsp;storyline&nbsp;of companies that are aiming to increase productivity and efficiency, whether that&rsquo;s more efficiently skipping food or pushing buttons on a phone to get a car, or a snack, or anything really, send to your current location on demand. But at the end of the day, Nootrobox is&nbsp;really just a bet on a couple of larger trends: that subscription commerce will continue to become more common, and that nootropics and supplements in general will remain the growth industry analysts predict.
The bootstrapped, San Francisco-based startup&nbsp;has been testing the service via pre-order campaigns and sold out of its first production batch. They&rsquo;re now shipping to nine states in the U.S. (CA, NY, MA, FL, GA, WA, IL, RI and TX) and are&nbsp;looking into&nbsp;further distribution&nbsp;leads now.
